:topic/math-academy-id 260} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186060762 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060964 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n=10$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2=9.$ After processing our results, we compute the mean of this sample using the usual methods and get the following result:

$$
\overline{x}=12
$$

 

This is an unbiased estimate of the population mean $\mu.$ However, it is unsatisfactory because we have no information regarding its reliability.

For this reason, it's often more helpful to give a range of possible values for $\mu.$ In other words, instead of reporting a single estimate $\overline{x},$ we might instead report a so-called **confidence interval,** which is an interval of the form

$$
(\overline{x}-E, \: \overline{x}+E)
$$

 

where 

- $\overline{x}$ is our estimate of the population mean, and

- $E$ is some **margin of error**.

In addition, we need to give some indication regarding the reliability of our confidence interval. With this in mind, we will construct a $\boldsymbol{95\%}$ **confidence interval** for the population mean $\mu$. The precise meaning of this will become clear shortly." :tutorial/id #uuid "f8ebcc7b-ddba-56d2-bb41-07916f3c2d09" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6232 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "55b16e12-fb99-528d-a98f-9e754fd27b3a" :step/math-academy-id 37842 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060769}} {:db/id 17592186060763 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059823 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059382 :question/id #uuid "97c8f1dc-747e-5aa4-ab4f-eb809abb560e" :question/math-academy-id "e-10035"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fb626c84-db31-5e1b-90cb-3f5d13ee0af5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049014}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060050} {:db/id 17592186060053} {:db/id 17592186498533} {:db/id 17592186498542} {:db/id 17592186498559} {:db/id 17592186498580}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals From Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "bc49103b-afb3-574a-8efd-6910f8c3b320" :step/math-academy-id 37861 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060764}} {:db/id 17592186060764 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059824 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059383 :question/id #uuid "3189a42a-200e-5caa-bc76-6ac1f4ae424d" :question/math-academy-id "e-10039"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "27d20d28-3fba-5830-8bff-76e9a1c24bec" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060051} {:db/id 17592186060054} {:db/id 17592186498524} {:db/id 17592186498543} {:db/id 17592186498557} {:db/id 17592186498576}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals: Applications"} :step/id #uuid "32d40006-ed8e-530b-8e5f-6ec28697e1f4" :step/math-academy-id 37883} {:db/id 17592186060765 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060965 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've assumed that the underlying population is normally distributed. However, if we have a *sufficiently large* sample, then according to the central limit theorem, we can use the approximation

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \approx N(0,1).
$$

So, even though we might not know the underlying distribution, we can still use our formula for the confidence interval of the population mean $\mu{:}$

$$
\overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4b9c6c26-d589-5847-a384-c431ad44a125" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6245 :tutorial/title "Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "043270f2-b372-59f5-98a2-64919b13fa7b" :step/math-academy-id 37884 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060763}} {:db/id 17592186060766 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060966 :tutorial/content "It's important to be able to interpret confidence intervals correctly.

Imagine we conduct several independent random samples from a population. The mean of the sample will be different for each sample. Some values of $\overline{x}$ might lie close to the population mean $\mu,$ and some could lie further away.

Suppose we construct a $90\%$ confidence interval for each sample and plot them on the same diagram. We might get a picture similar to the one below.

![](images/fc/fc8dd707751cd9e1cb0da1bf618b6d7aed740fab875d8d49c7c89fc09b77321e.png)

In the diagram above, we see that nine out of ten of our confidence intervals contain $\mu,$ while one of them (the red one) does *not* contain the population mean $\mu.$ 

The idea is that if we construct many $90\%$ confidence intervals, one for each sample, then approximately $90\%$ of these confidence intervals will contain the population mean $\mu.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d71a924b-5f1e-5a89-a56b-d540a4a53d74" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6247 :tutorial/title "Interpreting Confidence Intervals"} :step/id #uuid "5f0968c6-9ace-5735-9d92-61ff226b832e" :step/math-academy-id 37890 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060765}} {:db/id 17592186060767 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059825 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059384 :question/id #uuid "3a166c80-cc70-5dd3-9dbe-2798dc882199" :question/math-academy-id "e-10046"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b90997d0-b563-5541-9fe2-36d7457da7b5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049180} {:db/id 17592186049652}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060052} {:db/id 17592186060055} {:db/id 17592186498501} {:db/id 17592186498508} {:db/id 17592186498518} {:db/id 17592186498562} {:db/id 17592186498573}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals From Normal Populations"} :step/id #uuid "3461449b-03e6-5f5d-aff8-7cec85835701" :step/math-academy-id 37913 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060766}} {:db/id 17592186060768 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060967 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $Z \sim N(0,1).$ 

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean

- $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $z$-score

- $E = z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/58/581fc2da88e4419e78389a1b5eedb127f590641d0b7ee21c489ed85184795b13.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{―}{x}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}, & \,\overset{―}{x}+{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "cdae1125-df9d-525c-823d-64f129c3ab6f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6275 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Known Population Variance"} :step/id #uuid "afbe0be3-1d3c-5408-9cda-36c61677f0fb" :step/math-academy-id 38032 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060767}} {:db/id 17592186060769 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060968 :tutorial/content "In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

By transforming $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable, we have

$$
Z = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1).
$$

We wish to find a $z$-interval that we're $95\%$ confident that the random variable $Z$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

![](images/50/50a0f49fe5c96ba3259832fbf1a0abcedffb342301ca069bb7b88d157a181019.png)

  

To help with the notation, we define a new parameter $\alpha.$ Since we're computing a $95\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.
$$

Notice that $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/3c/3cdfd2c72bf7fe65e5d1b584d46d4c846e74615e54c739a6d1ea990c95011a8a.png)

  

According to our diagram,

$$
P(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025.
$$

  

Using a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that $z_{0.025} \approx 1.96.$ Therefore,

$$
P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025.
$$

In other words,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.96<Z<1.96)=0.95.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, there is a $95\%$ probability that our random variable $Z$ will lie in the interval $(-1.96, 1.96).$

Now, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1.96< & \,Z<1.96 \\ -1.96< & \,\frac{\overset{―}{x}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}<1.96 \\ -1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\overset{―}{x}-\mu <1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ -\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,-\mu \,<-\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}> & \,\mu >\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\mu <\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\: \overline{x} + 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

Finally, substituting our values

$$
n=10, \qquad
\overline{x}=12, \qquad
\sigma=3,
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is 

$$
\big( 12- 1.859, \: 12 + 1.859 \big).
$$

 

Now that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "609f60a5-fbfd-5385-89e2-f80dd6281f39" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6398 :tutorial/title "Constructing Confidence Intervals"} :step/id #uuid "e659ed87-b26a-54f6-bb76-e98cf99a6b01" :step/math-academy-id 38686 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060768}}] :activity/title "Confidence Intervals for One Mean: Known Population Variance" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186059935} {:db/id 17592186060762 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060964 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n=10$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2=9.$ After processing our results, we compute the mean of this sample using the usual methods and get the following result:

The idea is that if we construct many $90\%$ confidence intervals, one for each sample, then approximately $90\%$ of these confidence intervals will contain the population mean $\mu.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d71a924b-5f1e-5a89-a56b-d540a4a53d74" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6247 :tutorial/title "Interpreting Confidence Intervals"} {:db/id 17592186060767 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059825 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059384 :question/id #uuid "3a166c80-cc70-5dd3-9dbe-2798dc882199" :question/math-academy-id "e-10046"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b90997d0-b563-5541-9fe2-36d7457da7b5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049180} {:db/id 17592186049652}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060052} {:db/id 17592186060055} {:db/id 17592186498501} {:db/id 17592186498508} {:db/id 17592186498518} {:db/id 17592186498562} {:db/id 17592186498573}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals From Normal Populations"} :step/id #uuid "3461449b-03e6-5f5d-aff8-7cec85835701" :step/math-academy-id 37913 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060766}} {:db/id 17592186060768 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060967 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $Z \sim N(0,1).$ 

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean

- $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $z$-score

- $E = z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/58/581fc2da88e4419e78389a1b5eedb127f590641d0b7ee21c489ed85184795b13.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{―}{x}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}, & \,\overset{―}{x}+{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "cdae1125-df9d-525c-823d-64f129c3ab6f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6275 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Known Population Variance"} :step/id #uuid "afbe0be3-1d3c-5408-9cda-36c61677f0fb" :step/math-academy-id 38032 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060767}} {:db/id 17592186060967 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "cdae1125-df9d-525c-823d-64f129c3ab6f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6275 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Known Population Variance"} {:db/id 17592186060968 :tutorial/content "In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

By transforming $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable, we have

$$
Z = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1).
$$

We wish to find a $z$-interval that we're $95\%$ confident that the random variable $Z$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

![](images/50/50a0f49fe5c96ba3259832fbf1a0abcedffb342301ca069bb7b88d157a181019.png)

  

To help with the notation, we define a new parameter $\alpha.$ Since we're computing a $95\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.
$$

Notice that $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/3c/3cdfd2c72bf7fe65e5d1b584d46d4c846e74615e54c739a6d1ea990c95011a8a.png)

  

According to our diagram,

$$
P(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025.
$$

  

Using a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that $z_{0.025} \approx 1.96.$ Therefore,

$$
P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025.
$$

In other words,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.96<Z<1.96)=0.95.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, there is a $95\%$ probability that our random variable $Z$ will lie in the interval $(-1.96, 1.96).$

Now, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1.96< & \,Z<1.96 \\ -1.96< & \,\frac{\overset{―}{x}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}<1.96 \\ -1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\overset{―}{x}-\mu <1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ -\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,-\mu \,<-\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}> & \,\mu >\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\mu <\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\: \overline{x} + 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

Finally, substituting our values

$$
n=10, \qquad
\overline{x}=12, \qquad
\sigma=3,
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is 

$$
\big( 12- 1.859, \: 12 + 1.859 \big).
$$

 

Now that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "609f60a5-fbfd-5385-89e2-f80dd6281f39" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1. $\mathcal{A}\cong\mathcal{B}$
2. $\mathcal{B}\cong\mathcal{C}$
3. $\mathcal{C}\cong\mathcal{A}$

![](images/a1/a13f283489521fc43d73a5a128b79ff937dca760c8cea330706efe6f39ac26f6.png)" :question/worked-solution "In general, congruent polygons have the same shape. In other words:

- they have the same number of sides,
- all corresponding sides are congruent, and
- all corresponding interior angles are congruent.

With that in mind, let's compare the given polygons.

- Statement I is true. Since the polygons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ have the same number of sides and all corresponding sides and angles are congruent, we conclude that $\mathcal{A}\cong\mathcal{B}$.
- Statement II is false. Notice that the polygons $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ have the same number of sides, but they don't seem to have the same shape. In particular, we notice they don't have corresponding congruent angles ($\mathcal{B}$ does not have right angles, while $\mathcal{C}$ does).
- Statement III is false. By the same reasoning as above, we can see that the polygons $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ are not congruent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186111066 :question/id #uuid "91a11ae7-a2ba-5d78-b48c-5a0179c66090" :question/math-academy-id "q-25882"} {:db/id 17592186111093 :question/id #uuid "de8441f9-b5b3-54ab-a25c-529c00dca814" :question/math-academy-id "q-26504" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186110791 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "30fc8daf-a6eb-537b-b19b-06ad5504b5e6" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Congruent Polygons Given Side and Angle Measures"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "89c746ad-1610-5931-ab5c-45bb4f97b7a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186108318} {:answer/id #uuid "934b17a8-94aa-5fb3-b0f6-3650cb25a4f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186108319} {:answer/id #uuid "c870e598-a227-564b-a0a9-1e23e5654d6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186108320} {:answer/id #uuid "028ecd1f-f636-5e81-8aaf-126986c2bd32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186108321} {:answer/id #uuid "74ca8c5b-bfb1-58ef-b546-5092219f4348" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186108322}] :answer-field/id #uuid "38e76745-24d5-5762-8d5c-0a948cb43c06" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186108317}] :question/problem "![](images/fa/fa57e1d088e5384cfd7a08d524877e6a9fafce413f0b3039d59d90dd074d361b.png)

Write down a correct congruence statement for the quadrilaterals shown in the diagram above." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $\angle A \cong \angle C$.

Let's determine the vertices in the second quadrilateral that correspond to $A$. First, notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB &= XY \\
AD &= XW \\
&= ∠A \mid ≅∠X
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

- vertex $A$ corresponds to vertex $X$, and
- vertex $C$ corresponds to vertex $Z$ (since $C$ is opposite $A$ and $Z$ is opposite $X$).

As for the other two vertices, notice we have two more pairs of congruent angles:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}∠B & ≅∠Y \\ ∠D & ≅∠W\end{bmatrix}
$$

Similarly, we have two more pairs of congruent sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
CD &= ZW \\
BC &= YZ
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

- vertex $B$ corresponds to $Y$, and
- vertex $D$ corresponds to $W$.

Finally, we conclude that a correct congruence statement is

![](images/f1/f133fecf2229bc78933ad0e73bb707dd17cad45ae087037b3a327e3ef4dbbc73.png)" :question/worked-solution "The statement $ABCDE \cong PQRST$ means that $\mathcal R$ and $\mathcal Q$ are congruent. Moreover,

- vertex $A$ corresponds to vertex $P$,
- vertex $B$ corresponds to vertex $Q$,
- vertex $C$ corresponds to vertex $R$,
- vertex $D$ corresponds to vertex $S$,
- vertex $E$ corresponds to vertex $T$.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
CD &= RS \\
x &= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
m∠A &= m∠P \\
82^{∘} &= (11y + 5)^{∘} \\
77 &= 11y \\
7 &= y
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
x+y = 2+7=9
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048673} {:db/id 17592186111063 :question/id #uuid "b3a9d45a-5309-5015-a18f-4caacf6b1bfc" :question/math-academy-id "q-25856"} {:db/id 17592186111294 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186111783 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111851 :tutorial/content "Two polygons are **congruent** if they have the same shape. This means that

- they have the same number of sides,
- all corresponding sides are congruent, and
- all corresponding interior angles are congruent.

Consider the two polygons $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ below. Are they congruent?

![](images/b0/b0a11815bf9006ccdca0ebe71ff7ba53ac7526c71a715ece71914b103b4a24a8.png)

Let's check these criteria for our polygons $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$. We can see that both polygons have $3$ sides, and
$\begin{bmatrix}AB^(―) & ≅XY^(―), & AC^(―) & ≅XZ^(―), & BC^(―) & ≅YZ^(―), \\ ∠X & ≅∠A, & ∠Y & ≅∠B, & ∠Z & ≅∠C\end{bmatrix}$.
Therefore, the polygons are congruent, and we can write
$ABC \cong XYZ$.

The order in which we write the symbols is important: the corresponding vertices have to be in the same order.

We can also write $\mathcal{P} \cong \mathcal{Q}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "e6be6893-a7ca-578a-9510-8a8c2166e89b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2293 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Determine if the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-4I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable."} {:db/id 17592186323876 :question/id #uuid "22d45558-5d6d-54db-98ed-1c94a3458111" :question/math-academy-id "q-37085"} {:db/id 17592186323926 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 12 & 5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ \\ -3 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the second column of the matrix $P.$" :question/worked-solution "From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 12 & 5\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ 12 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ 12 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].$"} {:db/id 17592186125030 :question/id #uuid "6f7410b2-d03a-51b8-bc6b-c6a21e9f2fab" :question/math-academy-id "q-37084"} {:db/id $$

$$

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$

17592186125538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/9d/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](images/ca/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](images/3e/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](images/86/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f56a4e0-1c9c-573c-95a9-92a93682f0a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0dec286b-a54f-500f-b0be-886c4e33f4ba" :step/math-academy-id 31836 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125544}} {:db/id 17592186125539 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125840 :tutorial/content "There is a theorem that states the following:

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](images/e1/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fbab2132-0247-5376-a13b-df70908230d9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5084 :tutorial/title "Diagonalizable vs. Non-Diagonalizable Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "620e7d54-99b9-517c-83f8-d408a4768c65" :step/math-academy-id 31837 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125540}} {:db/id 17592186125540 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124599 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124411 :question/id #uuid "f7b85641-289b-57b2-9ffc-ff4c5e10025a" :question/math-academy-id "e-8572"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d3d7cb0b-7d81-55a5-9781-dda7e9cc9fb9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048775} {:db/id 17592186050001}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125086} {:db/id 17592186125088} {:db/id 17592186272005} {:db/id 17592186272006} {:db/id 17592186323864} {:db/id 17592186323876} {:db/id 17592186323926} {:db/id 17592186348381} {:db/id 17592186348382} {:db/id 17592186348383} {:db/id 17592186379810} {:db/id 17592186455441}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable"} :step/id #uuid "62cef711-c61d-5145-9dcc-a1e378b6208e" :step/math-academy-id 31838 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125541}} {:db/id 17592186125541 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125841 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is a diagonalizable matrix, then we can write

$$
A=PDP^{-1}.
$$

 

We can write this equation in an equivalent form, making $D$ the subject.

First, we left-multiply both sides of the equation by $P^{-1}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}\cdot A & ={P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & ={I}_{2}D{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & =D{P}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we right-multiply both sides of the equation by $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1}A\cdot P & =D{P}^{-1}\cdot P \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D{I}_{2} \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=PDP^{-1}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
D = P^{-1}A P.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e0a81c7-a393-5e5d-b8c1-16d982404f1a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5085 :tutorial/title "The Connection Between a Matrix and Its Diagonal Form"} :step/id #uuid :step/next {:db/id 17592186125539}} {:db/id 17592186125545 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125842 :tutorial/content "Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization 

![](images/76/76843143729d2bc62fc74dc6f03c24eb6a12dfc16a2609a8f2b36499cf39ce90.svg)

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

![](images/de/dec5fece3d89eaa022b4e951e63259b0f87213997397b1f8a91fb8fdabed0f74.svg)

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns." :tutorial/id #uuid "eb055132-9c7d-55a5-a2c6-0bcb54877c1c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5086 :tutorial/title "Uniqueness of the Diagonalization"} :step/id #uuid "a11b9aec-3c2f-5a01-8b7c-600351ec33e2" :step/math-academy-id 31854 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125662}} {:db/id 17592186125662 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125896 :tutorial/content "Let ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) be a diagonalizable ![](images/25/2521651122403a440e682fef383af333958f5b0d1334abe8b0771865d4daf100.svg) matrix. Then we can write
![](images/d8/d8f75220bef8327a8dfc49a6ae22e79c6f1649aefdc8fb43065e0616975a8c5c.svg)
where

- ![](images/1a/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) is an invertible matrix whose columns are eigenvectors ![](images/13/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](images/d0/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) of ![](images/c2/c2c85081d1f89d74b8ebb2761496d211d7052193809b7864e7983437f5d0b80f.svg) and

- ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the corresponding eigenvalues ![](images/ff/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and ![](images/4a/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

To understand this better, we need to distinguish between two coordinate systems.

In ![](images/fb/fb3130e489fdca80d1a077702861c20532fe613f9942d48fa1ec24055494a383.svg) the **standard basis** is
![](images/d2/d29d3ee4ae42a8d4ee5304cb0d29c6c811838d7b893a3a831b1b1b8b3af12561.svg)

So, if a vector is written as
![](images/bb/bbbc0379f1691a30dec4c34ec6171db1f116bec12a24891169957af68164f8d3.svg)
then ![](images/12/12adb8ba7ed45d89c9d9a80eb7c06616c41999e9fac57732bc24d2b55e1f8073.svg) The numbers ![](images/34/349015631ec44ef653936c85586d2c5ef56ba64392b3f92b4b92cbef3e731bc5.svg) and ![](images/a7/a77a353782459b753313d80235712695d65dc4a44d8d357aa41add6729f81d8f.svg) are the *standard coordinates* of ![](images/1f/1f3d1a60926323e963d7563529669e5cf8210771c8cbb0379f7a7d90e7c6aeec.svg)

Now let
![](images/58/58cdfb66e4c93d643fb97273610b3bbf67c8831516d4ccfc5b7790d55a169b28.svg)

Since the columns of ![](images/1a/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) are ![](images/13/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](images/d0/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) written in standard coordinates, the matrix ![](images/1a/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) converts coordinates from the basis ![](images/be/be2d796b77bebb31c0c06cef6af82bc9fb606a584a52cc5385cd32c4e143236c.svg) to the standard basis.

So, for any vector ![](images/b2/b2cb236f7a7f426f303b1391f76900b47f7d2fa1ad9c8110d8584182559017fd.svg)
![](images/7e/7e5a6a4b9bee9550e68c75a3945ad25d41f1de6dd3b089ce89005428da169f9d.svg)

Here, ![](images/4f/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) denotes the standard-coordinate column of the vector, while ![](images/3f/3f7132e53e5a27bee4c84bdddbac07971ec44ce12539c0e0c23bf0006057e199.svg) denotes the coordinate column of the same vector in the eigenvector basis ![](images/8d/8d16f7d70344ddea7a4fe48105e5ea75b984f48fd77f6f6eb89d26ad91b65805.svg)

Also, in the basis ![](images/da/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg) the eigenvectors have especially simple coordinate columns:
![](images/9f/9f5fec87a4253a3a1741c3380e2c6f9331928883ab2083dc02bf0e8efda6a98a.svg)

This is because
![](images/30/306d2bb3211dac2883b1eb6abaed54259272a8bcc6a4e562ff5da6fc52dee520.svg)

So, in the basis ![](images/da/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg) the matrix ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) acts by scaling the first coordinate by ![](images/ff/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and the second coordinate by ![](images/4a/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

We can summarize this process for any vector ![](images/4f/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) as a sequence of three steps:

- first, rewrite ![](images/4f/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) in the eigenvector basis ![](images/da/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg)

- then, apply the diagonal matrix ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) in that basis,

![](images/14/1459b0643f99c186f9710118617f89f34a601526e7154213471404d2feb2aaeb.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "61524e43-2735-5e5a-904b-2c4973df94a9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7958 :tutorial/title "Diagonalization as a Change of Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "831d0bbd-aa17-5012-9d8b-073e0d2d67a6" :step/math-academy-id 45769}] :activity/title "Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124753} {:db/id 17592186125538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/9d/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](images/ca/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](images/3e/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](images/86/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f56a4e0-1c9c-573c-95a9-92a93682f0a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0dec286b-a54f-500f-b0be-886c4e33f4ba" :step/math-academy-id 31836 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125544}} {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](images/e1/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fbab2132-0247-5376-a13b-df70908230d9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5084 :tutorial/title "Diagonalizable vs. Non-Diagonalizable Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "620e7d54-99b9-517c-83f8-d408a4768c65" :step/math-academy-id 31837 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125540}} {:db/id 17592186125840 :tutorial/content "There is a theorem that states the following:

$$
A=PDP^{-1}.
$$

 

We can write this equation in an equivalent form, making $D$ the subject.

First, we left-multiply both sides of the equation by $P^{-1}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}\cdot A & ={P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & ={I}_{2}D{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & =D{P}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we right-multiply both sides of the equation by $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1}A\cdot P & =D{P}^{-1}\cdot P \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D{I}_{2} \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=PDP^{-1}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
D = P^{-1}A P.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e0a81c7-a393-5e5d-b8c1-16d982404f1a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5085 :tutorial/title "The Connection Between a Matrix and Its Diagonal Form"} :step/id #uuid "0692f7d4-6f83-540e-bf5f-78b4908292bd" :step/math-academy-id 31841 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125542}} {:db/id 17592186125841 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is a diagonalizable matrix, then we can write

find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "260bb0c0-f4cc-5171-8f8e-251abb929092" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436963}} {:db/id 17592186436963 :step/content {:db/id 17592186404114 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20692b0c-ecf3-5857-b371-5e00dd088456" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ and

$P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186404120}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404120} :answer-field/id #uuid "5324a7ce-971d-53cb-b107-19a127a08e1f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404115}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f53e1d4c-a53d-5c3e-8ae8-0e080a8e331f" :question/math-academy-id "q-80496" :question/problem "Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c086434a-2e61-5437-a45d-1dd3277fb4b0"} {:db/id 17592186436964 :step/content {:db/id 17592186348376 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5b5beb30-0a75-5fc1-9136-9135683b1b51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346129} {:answer/id #uuid "70a5b71d-efb0-58ab-af42-12eed66f2bb6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346339} {:answer/id #uuid "783aadac-abc2-5341-8883-bae757b2fee4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -11\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346406} {:answer/id #uuid "78aeeb6e-6d38-58dc-93e3-4da1e56572c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346408} {:answer/id #uuid "df14a525-a2b3-5a1d-8fb5-695c415e41e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186347312}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186347312} :answer-field/id #uuid "feb4a3c4-e3c2-59e1-b4f8-a58de2ef0e9a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186348050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e9500f77-53af-537c-9030-31932253fda8" :question/math-academy-id "q-80372" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and

Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix." :question/worked-solution "Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

Therefore, we get

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-4I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "260bb0c0-f4cc-5171-8f8e-251abb929092" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436963}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15560ba1-c0e7-57a3-bd24-dc19e7e9f52a" :answer/type {:db/id **Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ 2 & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ 2 & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=15,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=15.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=3,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=1.$"} :step/id #uuid "e96641df-6f79-5c48-8011-c2641ddec815" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484302}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fb0eb10f-8358-5f70-9dcf-5a12623a7ffa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]$ and

"![](images/fa/fae88c8da0b50da2bc025cbac0dbc376be3b67b69b59823746873c6e7d102dcc.png)

Find the differential equation governing the current $I$ (in amperes) at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The circuit is a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\cos(4t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor of resistance $30\,\Omega,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.002\,\textrm{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $5\,\textrm{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C=\dfrac{q}{C}=\dfrac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence,

$$
V_L = 5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
6\cos(4t)=30I+500q+5\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(30I+500q+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -24\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =30\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500\,\frac{dq}{dt}+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t},$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+6\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+100I=-\dfrac{24}{5}\sin(4t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186231577 :question/id #uuid "6c2c7cc0-6b5e-525e-9e79-08e37b20c7d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-343955" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231407 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "![](images/48/4852aaf3945331346a68fe3f967658665f71d81be0e28fd0d34fd965c7045596.png)

Find the differential equation governing the current $I$ (in amperes) at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.005\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=10I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)=10I+200q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(10I+200q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 24\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+200\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+100I=12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186372939 :question/id #uuid "6e3c2b91-c3fb-5bb4-812b-cc5617342d2a" :question/math-academy-id "q-345253"} {:db/id 17592186372946 :question/id #uuid "f85e26f7-62ec-57fc-9951-f0dd8d7a7ebd" :question/math-academy-id "q-345256"} {:db/id 17592186231408 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231298 :question/id #uuid "6f2eeea4-7339-5f96-b3e0-fa160a791034" :question/math-academy-id "e-21895"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c6faa97d-4d8e-5d67-bb99-8aae6de5a840" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048130}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231579 :question/id #uuid "41513257-d21d-591d-a3aa-29569ac81171" :question/math-academy-id "q-343985"} {:db/id 17592186231583 :question/id #uuid "ac407737-c497-5620-a022-43410b01e805" :question/math-academy-id "q-344036"} {:db/id 17592186372841 :question/id #uuid "5c73c1ec-47f9-5904-a0c9-3ba0a4220384" :question/math-academy-id "q-344046"} {:db/id 17592186372918 :question/id #uuid "0fe4da9b-3724-51c1-9459-24000ff26a62" :question/math-academy-id "q-345229"} {:db/id 17592186372925 :question/id #uuid "ec7eedce-fc35-5301-816a-4bb7cc4477d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-345230"} {:db/id 17592186372932 :question/id #uuid "c9acdec8-78fa-5121-85f5-7da3b379926b" :question/math-academy-id "q-345231"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving an Equation Governing the Current in an RCL Circuit: Constant EMF"} {:db/id 17592186231298 :question/id #uuid "6f2eeea4-7339-5f96-b3e0-fa160a791034" :question/math-academy-id "e-21895" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186231408 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c6faa97d-4d8e-5d67-bb99-8aae6de5a840" :knowledge-point/title "Solving an Equation Governing the Current in an RCL Circuit: Constant EMF"}] :question/problem "![](images/08/085fe02b43301629af58379289fc9d1c49c90e71a83e0dd33f491ecf4b21bfc8.png)

Find an equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\dfrac25\,\textrm{C}$ and the initial current is $\dfrac34\,\textrm{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The circuit is a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,\Omega,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\textrm{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $4\,\textrm{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 10I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C=\dfrac{q}{C}=\dfrac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence,

$$
V_L = 4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
9=10I+4q+4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9) & =\frac{d}{dt}(10I+4q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt}+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t},$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+\dfrac52\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I=e^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I=e^{-2t}$ and $I=e^{-t/2}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=Ae^{-2t}+Be^{-t/2}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\dfrac25\,\textrm{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\dfrac34\,\textrm{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}=\dfrac94-\dfrac52I-q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\dfrac34$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{9}{4}-\frac{5}{2}I(0)-q(0) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{4}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =-\frac{1}{40},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\dfrac34$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & =A{e}^{-2(0)}+B{e}^{-0/2} \\ \frac{3}{4} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
I'=-2Ae^{-2t}-\dfrac12Be^{-t/2}.
$$

Substituting in $I'(0)=-\dfrac1{40}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{40} & =-2A{e}^{-2(0)}-\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{-0/2} \\ -\frac{1}{40} & =-2A-\frac{1}{2}B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}=A+B \\ -\frac{1}{40}=-2A-\frac{1}{2}B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\dfrac{7}{30}$ and $B=\dfrac{59}{60}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\dfrac{7}{30}e^{-2t}+\dfrac{59}{60}e^{-t/2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048130} {:db/id 17592186231579 :question/id #uuid "41513257-d21d-591d-a3aa-29569ac81171" :question/math-academy-id "q-343985"} {:db/id 17592186231583 :question/id #uuid coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+6q=12.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{9}{20}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $\frac{9}{10}\,\text{A}.$" :question/worked-solution "The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+6q) & =\frac{d}{dt}(12) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+6\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+6I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t}$ and $I={e}^{-2t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+B{e}^{-2t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{9}{20}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{9}{10}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=12-5I-6q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{9}{10}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =12-5I(0)-6q(0) \\  & =12-5\cdot \frac{9}{10}-6\cdot \frac{9}{20} \\  & =\frac{24}{5},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{9}{10}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10} & =A{e}^{-3(0)}+B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ \frac{9}{10} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3t}-2B{e}^{-2t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=\frac{24}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{24}{5} & =-3A{e}^{-3(0)}-2B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ \frac{24}{5} & =-3A-2B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10}=A+B \\ \frac{24}{5}=-3A-2B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{33}{5}$ and $B=\frac{15}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{33}{5}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{15}{2}{e}^{-2t}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186372841 :question/id #uuid "5c73c1ec-47f9-5904-a0c9-3ba0a4220384" :question/math-academy-id "q-344046"} {:db/id 17592186372918 :question/id #uuid
